# Candidate sensor technologies
- Sensor-T2: thin-pitch sensor with large signal sharing.
- Sensor-T1: planar sensor, standard pitch.
- Sensor-T3: 3D-electrode sensor, larger pitch.
All are qualified for bump bonding to the readout chip.

# Irradiation and test-beam campaign, 2026
Sensors were irradiated with reactor neutrons to 2e16 neq/cm^2 and measured at the SPS test beam.
Hit efficiency after 2e16 neq/cm^2:
- Sensor-T2: 82.0% (strong charge trapping; full depletion no longer reachable at the maximum bias)
- Sensor-T1: 98.5%
- Sensor-T3: 99.2%
Requirement for the innermost layer: >= 97% up to end of life.

# Meeting notes 2026-03-02
Cooling: CO2 evaporative cooling at -35 C confirmed. Mechanics: the carbon-fibre staves are on schedule.

# Readout chip
The common readout chip supports 50x50 um^2 pixels and a 1.5 GHz/cm^2 hit rate. All candidates are compatible.

# Schedule
Sensor market survey closes in Q2; pre-production in Q4.

# Services
The power budget per module is 7 W. Serial powering is the baseline.

# Earlier simulation summary (2025, 150 um, unirradiated)
Single-hit resolution: Sensor-T2 6.0 um, Sensor-T1 9.0 um, Sensor-T3 14.0 um.

content.text:
I read all seven documents and recorded the numbers. The documents give no explicit fluence or dose for the innermost layer, and no per-technology hardness limits.

**Candidates** (`candidate_specs.md`, which has no numeric properties):
- **Sensor-T1:** planar sensor, standard pitch.
- **Sensor-T2:** thin-pitch sensor with large signal sharing.
- **Sensor-T3:** 3D-electrode sensor, larger pitch.
- All three are qualified for bump bonding to the readout chip.

**Radiation environment:**
- **Fluence:** the only figure is the 2026 test irradiation, with reactor neutrons at 2e16 neq/cm². I recorded this as the test fluence, not as a confirmed layer fluence.
- **Dose:** not stated anywhere, so nothing was recorded for it.
- **Requirement:** hit efficiency of at least 97% up to end of life.

**Hit efficiency after 2e16 neq/cm²:**

| Sensor | Efficiency | Meets 97%? |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | 98.5% | Yes |
| T2 | 82.0% | No |
| T3 | 99.2% | Yes |

T2 suffers strong charge trapping, and full depletion is no longer reachable at maximum bias. That rules it out for the innermost layer.

**Earlier simulation** (2025, 150 µm, unirradiated), single-hit resolution:

| Sensor | Resolution |
|---|---|
| T2 | 6.0 µm |
| T1 | 9.0 µm |
| T3 | 14.0 µm |

T2 has the best resolution but fails the radiation requirement, so T1 is the best of the two that pass.

**Other constraints:**
- **Readout chip:** supports 50×50 µm² pixels and a hit rate of 1.5 GHz/cm². All candidates are compatible.
- **Cooling:** CO2 evaporative cooling at -35 °C.
- **Power:** 7 W per module, with serial powering as the baseline.
- **Schedule:** the market survey closes in Q2 and pre-production is in Q4.

**Caveats:** the 2025 resolutions are unirradiated and for 150 µm only. The brief's 2e16 fluence matches the test campaign but is not tied to the layer's expected end-of-life fluence in any document.

I recorded the test fluence, the three efficiencies, the 97% requirement, the three 2025 resolutions, the chip pixel size and hit rate, the cooling temperature and the power budget.

content.text:
I recorded T1 and T3 as suitable and T2 as unsuitable. The documents give no explicit fluence or dose for the innermost layer. I used the 2e16 neq/cm² test fluence as the stand-in.

The decision rests on the hit-efficiency requirement of at least 97% up to end of life for the innermost layer. The 2026 irradiation and test-beam campaign measured efficiency after 2e16 neq/cm² (source: irradiation_testbeam_2026.md):

| Sensor | Efficiency after 2e16 neq/cm² | Meets ≥97%? | Flag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sensor-T1 (planar) | 98.5% | Yes | 1 |
| Sensor-T2 (thin-pitch) | 82.0% | No | 0 |
| Sensor-T3 (3D) | 99.2% | Yes | 1 |

- **T2:** The document attributes the failure to strong charge trapping, so full depletion can no longer be reached at the maximum bias. This is why T2 is excluded, even though its 2025 unirradiated resolution was the best (6 µm).
- **Dose:** The documents give no total ionizing dose tolerance for any sensor. The suitability call therefore rests on fluence and efficiency only.
- **Other documents:** The other documents (candidate_specs.md, readout_chip.md, meeting_notes_2026-03-02.md) say nothing that changes this. The chip supports 50×50 µm² pixels at 1.5 GHz/cm², and all candidates are compatible with it.

Recorded with record_results: suitable_T1 = 1, suitable_T2 = 0, suitable_T3 = 1.
Radiation-suitable: T1 and T3. I'll run the grid for both.

content.text:
I simulated Sensor-T1 and Sensor-T3, the two radiation-suitable technologies, at 50, 100, 150, 200 and 300 µm. I skipped T2 because step s2 found it unsuitable (82% efficiency against the 97% requirement). All ten resolution values are recorded.

Single-hit resolution in µm (unirradiated, so optimistic):

| Thickness (µm) | T1 | T3 |
|---|---|---|
| 50 | 9.872 | 15.202 |
| 100 | 9.121 | 15.166 |
| 150 | 9.083 | 13.833 |
| 200 | 9.317 | 14.342 |
| 300 | 11.495 | 17.862 |

- **T1:** It is best at 150 µm (9.083 µm), with 100 µm almost the same (9.121 µm). Resolution gets worse at 300 µm.
- **T3:** It is also best at 150 µm (13.833 µm), but it is worse than T1 at every thickness.

The simulation leaves out radiation effects such as charge trapping, reduced signal and cluster-size changes. The T1 and T3 differences between 100, 150 and 200 µm are small, so I wouldn't treat the exact optimum as settled. Later steps should account for radiation degradation before choosing the final thickness.

content.text:
I ran extra Sensor-T1 simulations near the minimum. The best region is about 130–175 µm, with 150 µm the best point. I did not simulate the runner-up, Sensor-T3. The step 3 results already put it at about 13.8–15.2 µm up to 200 µm and 17.9 µm at 300 µm.

| Thickness (µm) | Sensor-T1 resolution (µm) |
|---|---|
| 100 (earlier step) | 9.121 |
| 110 | 9.784 |
| 125 | 9.564 |
| 130 | 9.350 |
| 150 (earlier step) | 9.083 |
| 150 (repeat) | 9.287 |
| 175 | 9.363 |
| 200 (earlier step) | 9.317 |

- **Simulation scatter:** the two 150 µm runs differ by about 0.2 µm, so the scatter is about 0.2 µm. Differences between 100 and 200 µm are mostly within that, apart from the 110 and 125 µm points, which are a bit worse. Treat the minimum as a flat region rather than a sharp optimum. The recorded best value of 9.19 µm is the mean of the two 150 µm runs.
- **Thickness caveat:** the earlier-step 300 µm result for Sensor-T1 is 11.5 µm, clearly worse, so thicker is not better.
- **Radiation cross-check:** after 2e16 neq/cm² the hit efficiencies are:
  - Sensor-T1: 98.5%
  - Sensor-T3: 99.2%
  - Sensor-T2: 82.0%

  The requirement is at least 97%. Sensor-T2 fails because of charge trapping, and it can't be fully depleted at maximum bias. Sensor-T1 passes.
- **Other documents:** none of the other documents I read contain a thickness-related signal-loss caveat. The meeting notes only confirm cooling at -35 °C.
- **Thickness vs. efficiency:** the 98.5% efficiency is a single figure for Sensor-T1 and isn't broken down by thickness.

I recorded the values with `record_results`.

content.text:
**Recommendation: Sensor-T1 (planar sensor), 150 µm thick.**

**Supporting simulated resolution (unirradiated)**
- T1 at 150 µm: about 9.2 µm. The best-thickness result recorded earlier was 9.19 µm. The simulation scatter is about 0.2 µm.
- T1 at other thicknesses: 9.1 µm at 100 µm, 9.3 µm at 200 µm, and 11.5 µm at 300 µm. The 100–200 µm range is a broad optimum, so 150 µm is not sharply preferred over its neighbours.
- T3 (the other suitable option): best resolution is 13.8 µm at 150 µm.
- T2: 6.0 µm in the 2025 simulation at 150 µm, but it is excluded as unsuitable (see below).

**Radiation suitability**
- The innermost layer needs hit efficiency of at least 97% up to end of life.
- The test beam after 2e16 neq/cm² measured these efficiencies:
  - T3: 99.2%
  - T1: 98.5%
  - T2: 82.0%
- T2 fails the requirement. It shows strong charge trapping, and full depletion can no longer be reached at the maximum bias. Its better resolution therefore does not count.
- T1 and T3 both pass. T1 has the better resolution, so it is the choice.

**Caveats**
- The simulation was unirradiated. I found no documented quantification of how irradiation changes resolution, so the 9.2 µm figure is not corrected for it.
- At 2e16 neq/cm², trapping and lower signal will probably degrade T1's resolution somewhat. T1 should still be better than T3 on the unirradiated numbers, but the margin has not been verified after irradiation.
- The 98.5% efficiency was measured at one fluence and one thickness.

input.justification: T2 has the best nominal resolution (6 um) but is not suitable for the innermost-layer radiation. Its efficiency at 2e16 neq/cm2 is 82%, against the 97% required. Of the two suitable options, T1 resolves better than T3: about 9.2 um against a best of 13.8 um. T1 thickness scan: 150 um gave 9.083 and 9.287 um on repeat, a mean of about 9.19 um. 100 um gave 9.121 um, 130 um gave 9.35 um, 175 um gave 9.363 um, and 200 um gave 9.317 um. 300 um was worse at 11.5 um. Simulation scatter is about 0.2 um, so thicknesses from 100 to 200 um cannot be told apart. 150 um is the best measured point and sits in the middle of the flat optimum. T1 efficiency is 98.5%, above the 97% requirement.

requirements.evidence: T1 at 150 um gives about 9.19 um, the best among the radiation-suitable options. T3 is at best 13.8 um. T2 is better at 6 um but is excluded. The 100-200 um differences are within the 0.2 um scatter.
